content_html:
04 Aug 2026 on C++, Game development

They gave me a Claude subscription and told me to get tokenmaxxing, so I tried to give it a fair shot.

It’s getting hard to avoid LLMs these days. Even if you avoid social media (or at least curate a follow list that avoids the bulk of the slop factory) and shrug off grandiose marketing statements that end up taken at face value in the news, it will likely come and find you at your place of work. Unlike the silver bullets of the past (like microservices or NoSQL), AI adoption seems to have been mandated in many places from the top layer of management, regardless of how many of them ever worked (or studied for) an engineering job.

I do admit that this approach immediately triggered my contrarian side and made me very defiant of any AI tool. I don’t believe someone who has never written a line of code in their life should be telling me what to use for my engineering job. This sounds to me like the most terminal case of micro-management, and that’s never a good thing (on top of being personally insulting).

Either way, over the past 3 months I got to use Claude and friends for work and I have to admit I found it somewhat useful. As long as you don’t ask it to write code. Please don’t ask it to write code. But I’m getting ahead of myself.

Artificial “Intelligence”

You probably heard this a million time by now, but artificial intelligence really isn’t that intelligent. It’s all marketing and buzzwords. All we really we have here is a (very) large neural network specialized in natural language processing.

As it turns out a lot of what we humans do on the computer is use text to communicate both ways, that model can be used to parse queries, generate textual1 responses based on a probabilistic heuristic or output command lines that can be then executed the old fashioned way and their results fed back into the model to make a loop until we reach some exit condition.

That’s not to say this is inherently bad. But it’s not magical either. “Agentic workflow” (or whatever they’re calling it at the time you’re reading this article) is just the realization that every software problem can be solved by adding another layer of indirection, and LLMs are no exception. If the neural network output can be improved by providing more input, then attach more input. And if the best way to figure out which input that would be is to query the model to generate a command and then pipe it through system(), so be it.

But let’s focus on the user point of view for the rest of this article.

We have Google at home…

There’s tons of valuable stuff out there on the internet. And assuming we do a decent job at keeping existing records intact, the net total sum of public knowledge can only improve (but, spoiler warning, there’s a caveat). The problem is finding it. This isn’t a new thing. I’m old enough to remember the time when you’d first get suggested to try this new “google” thing. But sadly it’s gotten quite worse since the 2000s golden age. They have been fighting an uphill battle against SEO for a while now, and it doesn’t look like they’re winning2.

Enter AI, as both a help and a hindrance. As a search tool, I have found it usually good at answering pointed questions expressed in natural language, especially given the conversational ability that allows refining the answer or bring up follow-up questions with the current context in mind. In practice it is the equivalent of running a bunch of searches, skimming through the top N links, and repeating until we think we’ve got the picture. Writing a short summary of a longer texts seems to be what LLMs are best at, and so it makes sense to use it to automate the process. Plus crawling and summarizing multiple searches is an inherently parallel job so it isn’t hard to see the efficiency that can be brought up by automating the process, assuming we have enough compute available and it doesn’t hallucinate the summaries, we’ll get back to both those points later because they are quite important.

The hindrance counterpart is of course that LLMs have lowered the cost of flooding the internet with word salad that dilutes an already precarious sea of information. Freya Holmér published a very good video on the topic and impact of littering the web with AI generated content in the never ending SEO arms race. Searching for information by hand is still an option today, especially if you already know reputable sources on a particular topic. But if you’re not, then a lot of care must be taken to sort out the slop from the real data, and automating it with an LLM loop may not help if you can’t instruct it which sources to keep and which to discard. Even before we talk about hallucinations, an LLM generated summary can only be as good as the sources it ingested.

…and now we also have Google at work

A particular area where I found an LLM loop useful for searching, that I haven’t found much discussion about so far, is internal company knowledge bases. Wherever you work, chances is there is a combination of wikis, slack conversation, Google Drives, Confluence pages and whatnot where a lot of good information is sitting but no one ever seems able to find it. I’ve experienced some of those “enterprise solutions” to be so bad that sometimes I couldn’t find a page I browsed a week before even when I typed the title (or what I remembered the title to be) in the search bar. I have written my share of internal technical article that I’m fairly sure no one ever found since, unless they kept a bookmark from the time I first linked it in the tech group chat.

In the past few months, and despite being new to the company, I have been able to find a bunch of answers that were written before my time. Because the same way “AI Google Search” can run multiple queries in parallel and summarize the answer, Claude and friends can turn my natural language question into a bunch of search queries for likely synonyms until they hit something. It proved really handy when I ran into a particular edge case with the engine and I could quickly search if someone ever reported it, offered a workaround or discussed why it had to behave this way. Every time you run into an issue in tech, chances are it’s been discussed before and you’re off a much better start if you can find that conversation.

This is technically not new tech. One of the things that has made Google and friends efficient for so long is that they automatically generate synonyms when building keyword metadata for a page. Your company wiki or chat search functions likely do not3. I suspect there is a lot of value sitting in year old slack conversation logs that are absurdly hard to access without an LLM to search for them, or a more veteran coworker being able to remember it and point you towards it.

Now is it efficient from a tech perspective to run an expensive LLM to search through a company wiki when they could instead implement basic search engine techniques that are decades old at this point? No, I’m fairly sure it is not. Indexing the content the way Google did 20 years ago with would definitely be a much more efficient solution, compute wise. But from a user perspective it is much more desirable than trying to search for “UI” and getting no results because the plaintext reads “User Interface” in the page they are looking for.

Hallucinations and false positives

Once an LLM has found an answer, it’s usually a good practice to go look at the primary source. Reading that article, document or chat log will help ensure the answer wasn’t hallucinated.

Hallucinations are an inherent property of how LLMs work. Token generation isn’t based on logic or truth, it’s based on statistics and from my understanding there is no way to entirely avoid them. I have experienced them on all models, from the cheap (and pretty bad) free version of Copilot that comes with Bing to the fanciest paid models of Claude.

I have found them most common when asking a very specific question that hasn’t be answered before, like asking for a particular niche feature in CMake or Vulkan or Xcode. Instead of answering “no it can’t be done”, I got the most probabilistic answer which suggested I try to click a button that wasn’t there or enable a feature flag that didn’t exist.

The whole thing is akin to asking someone who’s generally knowledgeable about a problem domain, but not the specific software or library you are using. They would reply “yeah that sounds like a thing you should be able to do” because it feels like a reasonable expectation to have and maybe is a feature in similar products. I suspect it’s the same reason why when writing code an LLM would try to call a non-existing API, because based on other languages it sounds like C++ containers should have a .sort() function. Because it’s the kind of thing you can do in Python and C#. That’s not the case because C++ makes a strong distinction between containers, iterators and algorithms, but LLMs do not reason (despite their marketing calling it “reasoning”) from first principles.

While this could be partially remedied by always asking for a primary source or citation, I dislike the idea that one has to add magical incantations to their queries to get the right results. It’s a good laugh to make fun of “make no mistake” memes, until you start having to consider similar things seriously. Plus models seem to get a new release every year or less, which would probably require the user to revise all their rituals (or watch them become pointless rituals that engineers do without remembering why).

Another issue I noted is that with connectors it’s somewhat easy to get the LLM to start feeding itself. For example when asked to find prior mentions of a recommendation I was writing for a client, Claude was adamant that this was supported by past reports… until it turned out one of those was the one I was actually writing. It was easy enough to catch because I had the breakdown with sources, but had it just gave me numbers I could easily have created a self-reinforcing loop. Likewise if coworkers were querying the same database and found my work-in-progress report, their summaries may have taken it as gospel. Again, those robots are anything but intelligent, and often you need to lay out some very basic things to avoid really stupid assumptions.

To finish on that topic, I also noticed a risk of telephone game happening with connectors that plug into another LLM. Once I got Claude telling me there was concrete evidence that a certain technical design was the result of a deliberate choice by the team, while it turned out it had taken the summary of another AI at face value, and the real primary source was two users speculating on why the module worked this way on the public forums. Again this is a tool that is good at summarizing data, but not always good at selecting which data to trust.

Coding?

Up until this paragraph my use cases have focused on research. But what about writing code? After all, it is the next big thing™️ and it’s coming any day now, isn’t it? Simply put: it’s not very good.

While I have found LLMs useful for researching and planning code changes, my attempts at actually making them write code have been quite lackluster. I found them to be slow and expensive to generate, for a mediocre result.

In one use case, after a long discussion, I asked it to make an optimization refactor where it would remove the Update() method of a MonoBehaviour derived object, put those objects inside a List<Foo> owned by a manager class and then run the equivalent update in the manager class as a for loop. This is a fairly common optimization in Unity games to avoid paying the cost of a (virtual) invocation of MonoBehaviour.Update() from the C++ part of the engine to the managed C# script when you have many objects of the same type.

Instead of doing just that, Claude created a GameUpdateable base class with an OnUpdate() method, made Foo inherit from it, then stored the array as List<GameUpdateable> in the manager and made a loop calling GameUpdateable.OnUpdate(). While this could still be devirtualized by some C# backends, and while using a pure C# call is still a win compared to a C++ to C# call, it was still a more complex and over-engineered solution than the one I had asked. Instead of “just doing the thing”, Claude had decided to apply some OOP design pattern that was uncalled for. And that wasn’t a really hard thing to do, the changes were localized to maybe 2 or 3 files.

Research tells me this is likely due to the fact that the training data for game development (and to some extent all native programming) is poor. Languages that favour OOP dominate the training data, even after applying some filtering weights.

Worse, when it comes to games, there are barely any primary sources available at all. The last AAA game to be open sourced was Doom 3, a title that released in 2004, 22 years ago. It doesn’t even have multithreading4! Other classics that have been released on Github over the years are usually from the 90s, complete with software rasterization or fixed pipeline OpenGL 1.2 if you’re lucky.

If you ask an LLM to write game code today, chances here it’s been trained on hobby projects, game jams and tutorial demos, assuming it’s been trained on games at all.

Friends who work on custom engines with bespoke scripting languages told me that most script they got out of LLMs was entirely at odds with the way they write it internally, because the only available training data for their in-house scripting language is found in mods.

Oh, and when I mentioned expensive, remember than outputs use 5 to 10 times more tokens than inputs (or maybe output tokens are priced 5-10x compared to input, which is the same). So while writing summaries is not too token-hungry because it ingests much more than it produces, asking it to write code is the opposite.

Coding assistant

I was recently reading about the work of British management consultant Stafford Beer 5. His whole field of management cybernetics6 can be very roughly summarized by the idea that a manager (and at a larger scale, a company) is limited in its ability to make good decisions by its capacity to process information about its own workings, its customers and suppliers and any other factors that can influence the outcomes. One important factor is that there is always more information (signal) coming in as the circumstances change and so if something cannot be processed, it will likely be dropped, and if too much is dropped (for example if you take the extreme case of reducing all inputs into a green or red signal), bad things happen. You need enough variety in the data that is acted upon to avoid missing something crucial.

In a similar (but imperfect, I’ll admit) analogy, dropping in a new codebase requires processing a lot of data to make the right call. That happens each time you change jobs or projects, and when you’re in the consulting business that could be quite frequent. And so, when trying to make an impact on a project in a short amount of time, one is often limited by how much information they can absorb. In those environments, having an LLM that can help exploring the code and pulling on some strings to see where they lead can be quite helpful. Maybe we should have kept with the original “AI coding assistant” name instead of trying to make them do everything…

I did use it to try and help me fix bugs, and again found it useful in areas where I didn’t know much since it helped my understanding of some code, but again I need to stress the need to double check everything. I can usually spot nonsensical claims when it comes to the things I’ve with before, but for new topics it’s much more dangerous.

To give some examples, I gave it a go on my personal rendering project and I got mixed results with the bugs I was trying to understand.

The first was a culling bug due to mixed-up handedness. I was fairly easy to find if, unlike me, you had not stubbornly refused to learned the first principles math behind it. I’m sure someone who’s been doing graphics for a few years would have caught it quickly. When asked it to write a fix, it came up with a textbook solution that worked, but was much less efficient than the project I had been taking inspiration from, despite Claude having parsed the source in its context.

The second was a PBR lighting issue that made it suggest we rewrite the whole lighting, move the main light position and add environment lighting, all to conclude after a few hours that one of the assets had a faulty metallic/roughness texture and no amount of changing the lighting code would fix it properly. Again, it’s easy to be led on a wild goose chase by a confident sounding LLM when you aren’t yourself an expert on the topic.

I keep this quote in mind a lot lately:

It's interesting how AI is constantly providing false information and incorrect statements about my area of expertise. Fortunately, it's very useful and always right about topics I know very little about.— pikuma.com (@pikuma) June 19, 2026

Sustainability

AI companies are all losing money. Of course they all have promises that they will eventually turn a profit and make an insane return on investments, but so far they haven’t. The tokens you get are making a marginal profit7, but overall they’re running at a loss. Given that hardware isn’t getting cheaper and models still need to be trained all the time, at the moment it doesn’t look like the current prices are sustainable.

That’s all to say that signs point towards the LLMs getting more expensive in the future, not less. Like every tool you can buy or rent to help you on the job, there should be a cost vs benefit calculation to be kept in mind, and so far it doesn’t seem to be happening outside of companies mandating everyone uses AI, followed by a counter order a few months later when the bills come due.

In a past life I had to argue every year to renew a license for a profiling tool that cost about 20 EUR a month. I’ve heard since that everyone at the company is now getting a Claude subscription, even non-programmers. This is the kind of decision that baffles me. Management will not trust its engineers to spend their money on the tools they say they need, but then will tell everyone they have to use a shiny expensive toy they didn’t request.

Is an LLM subscription more versatile than a profiler license for the average programmer? Probably. I found it useful to speed up research in areas I wasn’t familiar with. Would I use it every day if I was working on the same project all the time? Probably not. Did it radically change how I code? Not really. Is it going to replace programmers? I don’t think it’s there, and at this point I’m seriously doubting it ever will be.

And if you find yourself using it a lot to write boilerplate code that you don’t really care to review, maybe you need to invest in a better API.

1: I know that LLMs can also generate image and video formats. But it’s out of scope for the purpose of this article. Also the results suck. AI “art” is a non-starter in my book.

2: If you like cooking and sometimes search online for recipes, you know exactly what I mean.

3: Email on the other hand has seen some progress since the time where you had to install Google Desktop to be able to find anything in Outlook, probably because the biggest email providers today also run a search engine and an AI research division.

4: There’s some in the BFG edition that was made in 2012, but it’s more of a port than a new game.

5: If you’ve ever heard the phrase “the purpose of a system is what it does”, that’s him.

6: Beer was influenced by W. Ross Ashby, who himself built upon the works of Claude Shannon. Yes. that’s the Claude your LLM is named after. We’ve come full circle, in a way.

7: Meaning they’re profitable if only consider the direct costs of running the model, which excludes a lot of R&D and hardware spending.

I can usually spot nonsensical claims when it comes to the things I’ve with before, but for new topics it’s much more dangerous.To give some examples, I gave it a go on my personal rendering project and I got mixed results with the bugs I was trying to understand.The first was a culling bug due to mixed-up handedness. I was fairly easy to find if, unlike me, you had not stubbornly refused to learned the first principles math behind it. I’m sure someone who’s been doing graphics for a few years would have caught it quickly. When asked it to write a fix, it came up with a textbook solution that worked, but was much less efficient than the project I had been taking inspiration from, despite Claude having parsed the source in its context.The second was a PBR lighting issue that made it suggest we rewrite the whole lighting, move the main light position and add environment lighting, all to conclude after a few hours that one of the assets had a faulty metallic/roughness texture and no amount of changing the lighting code would fix it properly. Again, it’s easy to be led on a wild goose chase by a confident sounding LLM when you aren’t yourself an expert on the topic.I keep this quote in mind a lot lately:It's interesting how AI is constantly providing false information and incorrect statements about my area of expertise. Fortunately, it's very useful and always right about topics I know very little about.— pikuma.com (@pikuma) June 19, 2026SustainabilityAI companies are all losing money. Of course they all have promises that they will eventually turn a profit and make an insane return on investments, but so far they haven’t. The tokens you get are making a marginal profit7, but overall they’re running at a loss. Given that hardware isn’t getting cheaper and models still need to be trained all the time, at the moment it doesn’t look like the current prices are sustainable.That’s all to say that signs point towards the LLMs getting more expensive in the future, not less. Like every tool you can buy or rent to help you on the job, there should be a cost vs benefit calculation to be kept in mind, and so far it doesn’t seem to be happening outside of companies mandating everyone uses AI, followed by a counter order a few months later when the bills come due.In a past life I had to argue every year to renew a license for a profiling tool that cost about 20 EUR a month. I’ve heard since that everyone at the company is now getting a Claude subscription, even non-programmers. This is the kind of decision that baffles me. Management will not trust its engineers to spend their money on the tools they say they need, but then will tell everyone they have to use a shiny expensive toy they didn’t request.Is an LLM subscription more versatile than a profiler license for the average programmer? Probably. I found it useful to speed up research in areas I wasn’t familiar with. Would I use it every day if I was working on the same project all the time? Probably not. Did it radically change how I code? Not really. Is it going to replace programmers? I don’t think it’s there, and at this point I’m seriously doubting it ever will be.And if you find yourself using it a lot to write boilerplate code that you don’t really care to review, maybe you need to invest in a better API.1: I know that LLMs can also generate image and video formats. But it’s out of scope for the purpose of this article. Also the results suck. AI “art” is a non-starter in my book.2: If you like cooking and sometimes search online for recipes, you know exactly what I mean.3: Email on the other hand has seen some progress since the time where you had to install Google Desktop to be able to find anything in Outlook, probably because the biggest email providers today also run a search engine and an AI research division.4: There’s some in the BFG edition that was made in 2012, but it’s more of a port than a new game.5: If you’ve ever heard the phrase “the purpose of a system is what it does”, that’s him.6: Beer was influenced by W. Ross Ashby, who himself built upon the works of Claude Shannon. Yes. that’s the Claude your LLM is named after. We’ve come full circle, in a way.7: Meaning they’re profitable if only consider the direct costs of running the model, which excludes a lot of R&D and hardware spending.

blocks.html_en: Enter AI, as both a help and a hindrance. As a search tool, I have found it usually good at answering pointed questions expressed in natural language, especially given the conversational ability that allows refining the answer or bring up follow-up questions with the current context in mind. In practice it is the equivalent of running a bunch of searches, skimming through the top N links, and repeating until we think we’ve got the picture. Writing a short summary of a longer texts seems to be what LLMs are best at, and so it makes sense to use it to automate the process. Plus crawling and summarizing multiple searches is an inherently parallel job so it isn’t hard to see the efficiency that can be brought up by automating the process, assuming we have enough compute available and it doesn’t hallucinate the summaries, we’ll get back to both those points later because they are quite important.

blocks.html_en: The hindrance counterpart is of course that LLMs have lowered the cost of flooding the internet with word salad that dilutes an already precarious sea of information. blocks.html_en: I was recently reading about the work of British management consultant Stafford Beer 5. His whole field of management cybernetics6 can be very roughly summarized by the idea that a manager (and at a larger scale, a company) is limited in its ability to make good decisions by its capacity to process information about its own workings, its customers and suppliers and any other factors that can influence the outcomes. One important factor is that there is always more information (signal) coming in as the circumstances change and so if something cannot be processed, it will likely be dropped, and if too much is dropped (for example if you take the extreme case of reducing all inputs into a green or red signal), bad things happen. You need enough variety in the data that is acted upon to avoid missing something crucial.

content_html_zh:
2026 年 8 月 4 日关于 C++, 游戏开发

他们给了我一个 Claude 订阅，并告诉我要获得 tokenmaxxing，所以我试着给予它一个公平的机会。

如今，想要避开法学硕士越来越难了。 即使你避开社交媒体（或者至少策划一个关注列表，避开大量的污水工厂）并摆脱那些最终被新闻报道的浮夸营销声明，它很可能会来到你的工作地点找到你。 与过去的灵丹妙药（如微服务或 NoSQL）不同，人工智能的采用似乎在许多地方都是高层管理人员强制要求的，无论他们中有多少人曾经从事过（或学习过）工程工作。

我确实承认，这种方法立即触发了我的逆向思维，并使我对任何人工智能工具都非常蔑视。 我不相信那些一生中从未写过一行代码的人应该告诉我在我的工程工作中使用什么。 在我看来，这听起来像是微观管理的最极端案例，而且这从来都不是一件好事（除了个人侮辱之外）。

不管怎样，在过去的三个月里，我在工作中使用了 Claude 和朋友，我不得不承认我发现它有点用。 只要你不要求它写代码。 请不要要求它编写代码。 但我有点超前了。

人工智能”

你可能已经听过这句话一​​百万次了，但人工智能确实没有那么智能。 这都是营销和流行语。 我们真正拥有的只是一个（非常）大型的专门从事自然语言处理的神经网络。

事实证明，我们人类在计算机上所做的很多事情都是使用文本进行双向通信，该模型可用于解析查询、基于概率启发式生成文本响应或输出命令行，然后可以以老式方式执行这些命令行，并将其结果反馈到模型中以进行循环，直到达到某个退出条件。

这并不是说这本质上是不好的。 但这也不神奇。 “代理工作流程”（或者无论您在阅读本文时他们如何称呼它）只是认识到每个软件问题都可以通过添加另一层间接来解决，法学硕士也不例外。 如果可以通过提供更多输入来改善神经网络输出，则附加更多输入。 如果确定哪个输入的最佳方法是查询模型以生成命令，然后通过 system() 将其传输，那就这样吧。

但在本文的其余部分，让我们重点关注用户的观点。

我们家里有谷歌...

互联网上有大量有价值的东西。 假设我们在保持现有记录完整方面做得不错，那么公共知识的净总量只会有所提高（但是，剧透警告，有一个警告）。 问题是找到它。 这不是什么新鲜事。 我已经足够大了，还记得你第一次被建议尝试这个新的“谷歌”东西的时候。 但遗憾的是，自 2000 年代黄金时代以来，情况变得更加糟糕。 他们与 SEO 进行一场艰苦的战斗已经有一段时间了，但看起来他们并没有获胜2。

人工智能的出现，既是一种帮助，也是一种阻碍。 作为一种搜索工具，我发现它通常擅长回答以自然语言表达的尖锐问题，特别是考虑到其对话能力可以改进答案或在考虑当前上下文的情况下提出后续问题。 在实践中，这相当于运行一堆搜索，浏览前 N 个链接，然后重复，直到我们认为我们已经得到了图片。 撰写较长文本的简短摘要似乎是法学硕士最擅长的事情，因此使用它来自动化该过程是有意义的。 另外，爬行和总结多个搜索本质上是一项并行工作，因此不难看出自动化流程可以带来的效率，假设我们有足够的可用计算并且它不会产生幻觉摘要，我们稍后会回到这两点，因为它们非常重要。

当然，与之对应的障碍是，法学硕士降低了互联网上充斥着大量词汇的成本，这些词汇稀释了本已岌岌可危的信息海洋。 Freya Holmér 发布了一段非常好的视频，主题是在永无休止的 SEO 军备竞赛中，人工智能生成的内容在网络上乱扔垃圾的主题和影响。 如今，手动搜索信息仍然是一种选择，特别是如果您已经了解特定主题的信誉良好的来源。 但如果你不这样做，那么就必须非常小心地从真实数据中剔除溢出，并且如果你无法指示它保留哪些来源以及丢弃哪些来源，那么使用 LLM 循环将其自动化可能无济于事。 甚至在我们谈论幻觉之前，法学硕士生成的摘要的好坏取决于它所吸收的来源。

......现在我们还有谷歌在工作

我发现 LLM 循环对于搜索很有用的一个特定领域是公司内部知识库，但到目前为止我还没有找到太多讨论。 无论您在哪里工作，很可能都会有 wiki、slackDialogue、Google Drive、Confluence 页面以及诸如此类的东西，其中有很多有用的信息，但似乎没有人能够找到它们。 我经历过一些“企业解决方案”非常糟糕，有时即使我在搜索栏中输入标题（或我记得的标题），也找不到一周前浏览过的页面。 我已经写了一篇内部技术文章，我相当确定自那以后再也没有人发现过，除非他们从我第一次在技术群聊中链接它时就保留了书签。

在过去的几个月里，尽管我是公司的新手，但我已经找到了很多在我之前写下的答案。 因为“人工智能谷歌搜索”可以并行运行多个查询并总结答案，所以克劳德和朋友们可以将我的自然语言问题转化为一堆可能同义词的搜索查询，直到找到某些内容。 当我遇到引擎的特定边缘情况时，它确实很方便，我可以快速搜索是否有人报告过它，提供了解决方法或讨论了为什么它必须以这种方式运行。 每当您遇到技术问题时，很可能以前已经讨论过该问题，如果您能找到该对话，那么您就有了一个更好的开始。

从技术上讲，这并不是新技术。 长期以来，谷歌和朋友们保持高效的原因之一是，他们在为页面构建关键字元数据时自动生成同义词。 您公司的 wiki 或聊天搜索功能可能不会3。 我怀疑，一年前的松弛对话日志中蕴含着很多价值，如果没有法学硕士来搜索这些日志，或者没有经验丰富的同事能够记住它并为你指明方向，这些日志就很难访问。

现在，从技术角度来看，当他们可以实施已有数十年历史的基本搜索引擎技术时，运行昂贵的法学硕士来搜索公司维基是否有效？ 不，我相当确定不是。 从计算角度来看，像 Google 20 年前那样对内容建立索引肯定是一个更高效的解决方案。 但从用户的角度来看，这比尝试搜索“UI”却得不到结果要好得多，因为他们正在寻找的页面中明文显示的是“用户界面”。

幻觉和误报

一旦法学硕士找到答案，通常最好去查看主要来源。 阅读该文章、文档或聊天记录将有助于确保答案不是幻觉。

幻觉是法学硕士工作方式的固有属性。 代币生成不是基于逻辑或真理，而是基于统计数据，根据我的理解，没有办法完全避免它们。 我在所有型号上都体验过它们，从 Bing 附带的便宜（而且相当糟糕）的 Copilot 免费版本到 Claude 最奇特的付费型号。

我发现它们在询问以前没有得到解答的非常具体的问题时最常见，例如询问 CMake、Vulkan 或 Xcode 中的特定利基功能。 我没有回答“不，这是不可能的”，而是得到了最有可能的答案，该答案建议我尝试单击不存在的按钮或启用不存在的功能标志。

整个事情类似于询问通常了解某个问题领域的人，但不了解您正在使用的特定软件或库。 他们会回答“是的，这听起来像是你应该能够做的事情”，因为这感觉像是一个合理的期望，并且可能是类似产品的一个功能。 我怀疑这与 LLM 在编写代码时尝试调用不存在的 API 的原因相同，因为基于其他语言，听起来 C++ 容器应该有一个 .sort() 函数。 因为这是你可以用 Python 和 C# 做的事情。 事实并非如此，因为 C++ 在容器、迭代器和算法之间做出了强烈的区分，但法学硕士不会从第一原理出发进行推理（尽管他们的营销称之为“推理”）。

虽然这可以通过始终询问主要来源或引文来部分解决，但我不喜欢这样的想法：人们必须在查询中添加神奇的咒语才能获得正确的结果。 在你开始认真考虑类似的事情之前，取笑“不要犯错”模因是一件很好的事。 另外，模型似乎每年或更短时间都会发布一个新版本，这可能需要用户修改所有的仪式（或者看着它们变成工程师不记得为什么而做的毫无意义的仪式）。

我注意到的另一个问题是，使用连接器，让法学硕士开始自我喂养有点容易。 例如，当被要求查找之前提到的我为客户撰写的推荐时，克劳德坚称这得到了过去报告的支持…… 直到事实证明其中一篇是我真正写的。 它很容易被发现，因为我对来源进行了故障，但如果它只是给了我数字，我可以很容易地创建一个自我强化的循环。 同样，如果同事查询同一个数据库并找到我的正在进行的工作报告，他们的摘要可能会将其视为福音。 再说一次，这些机器人一点也不智能，通常你需要布置一些非常基本的东西，以避免真正愚蠢的假设。

最后，我还注意到插入另一个法学硕士的连接器存在电话游戏的风险。 当克劳德告诉我时，有确凿的证据表明某个技术设计是团队深思熟虑的选择的结果，而事实证明它是从另一个人工智能的表面上总结出来的，而真正的主要来源是两个用户在公共论坛上猜测为什么该模块会这样工作。 同样，这是一个擅长总结数据的工具，但并不总是擅长选择值得信任的数据。

编码？

直到本段为止，我的用例都集中在研究上。 但是写代码呢？ 毕竟，它是下一件大事™️，而且随时都会到来，不是吗？ 简单地说：这不是很好。

虽然我发现法学硕士对于研究和规划代码更改很有用，但我实际上让他们编写代码的尝试却相当乏善可陈。 我发现它们的生成速度慢且成本高，而且结果平庸。

在一个用例中，经过长时间的讨论，我要求它进行优化重构，它将删除 MonoBehaviour 派生对象的 Update() 方法，将这些对象放入管理器类拥有的 List<Foo> 中，然后在管理器类中作为 for 循环运行等效更新。 这是 Unity 游戏中相当常见的优化，以避免在拥有许多相同类型的对象时从引擎的 C++ 部分向托管 C# 脚本支付 MonoBehaviour.Update()（虚拟）调用的成本。

Claude 并没有这样做，而是创建了一个带有 OnUpdate() 方法的 GameUpdateable 基类，让 Foo 继承它，然后将数组作为 List<GameUpdateable> 存储在管理器中，并创建一个调用 GameUpdateable.OnUpdate() 的循环。 虽然这仍然可以通过某些 C# 后端进行去虚拟化，并且与 C++ 到 C# 调用相比，使用纯 C# 调用仍然是一种胜利，但它仍然是一个比我要求的解决方案更复杂和过度设计的解决方案。 克劳德没有“只是做事”，而是决定应用一些不需要的 OOP 设计模式。 这并不是一件很难的事情，更改可能只限于 2 或 3 个文件。

研究告诉我，这可能是因为游戏开发（以及某种程度上所有本机编程）的训练数据很差。 即使在应用了一些过滤权重之后，支持 OOP 的语言仍然在训练数据中占主导地位。

更糟糕的是，当谈到游戏时，几乎没有任何可用的主要来源。 最后一款开源的 AAA 游戏是《毁灭战士 3》，该游戏于 2004 年发布，距今已有 22 年了。 它甚至没有多线程4！ 多年来在 Github 上发布的其他经典作品通常来自 90 年代，如果幸运的话，还配有软件光栅化或固定管道 OpenGL 1.2。

如果你今天要求法学硕士编写游戏代码，假设它接受过游戏方面的培训，那么他很可能接受过业余爱好项目、游戏即兴创作和教程演示方面的培训。

使用定制脚本语言开发自定义引擎的朋友告诉我，他们从法学硕士获得的大多数脚本与他们内部编写的方式完全不一致，因为他们内部脚本语言唯一可用的训练数据是在 mod 中找到的。

哦，当我提到昂贵时，请记住输出使用的代币比输入多 5 到 10 倍（或者输出代币的价格可能是输入的 5-10 倍，这是相同的）。 因此，虽然编写摘要并不太需要令牌，因为它吸收的东西比产生的东西多得多，但要求它编写代码则相反。

编码助理

我最近读到了英国管理顾问斯塔福德·比尔 5 的著作。 他的整个管理控制论领域6可以非常粗略地概括为这样一个想法：管理者（以及更大范围内的公司）处理有关其自身运作、客户和供应商以及任何其他可能影响结果的因素的信息的能力限制了其做出正确决策的能力。 一个重要的因素是，随着情况的变化，总会有更多的信息（信号）进入，因此如果某些内容无法处理，它很可能会被丢弃，如果丢弃太多（例如，如果您采取将所有输入减少为绿色或红色信号的极端情况），就会发生不好的事情。 您需要所处理的数据有足够的多样性，以避免遗漏一些重要的内容。

在一个类似的（但我承认不完美）类比中，放入新的代码库需要处理大量数据才能做出正确的调用。 每次你换工作或项目时，这种情况都会发生，当你从事咨询业务时，这种情况可能会非常频繁。 因此，当试图在短时间内对一个项目产生影响时，人们往往会受到他们能够吸收多少信息的限制。 在这些环境中，拥有一个法学硕士可以帮助探索代码并拉动一些字符串以了解它们的走向，这会非常有帮助。 也许我们应该保留原来的“人工智能编码助手”名称，而不是试图让他们做所有的事情……

我确实用它来尝试帮助我修复错误，并再次发现它在我不太了解的领域很有用，因为它有助于我理解一些代码，但我再次需要强调需要仔细检查所有内容。 当涉及到我以前处理过的事情时，我通常可以发现无意义的主张，但对于新主题来说，这要危险得多。

举一些例子，我在我的个人渲染项目中尝试了一下，得到的结果与我试图理解的错误混合在一起。

第一个是由于左右手的混合导致的剔除错误。 如果你没有像我一样顽固地拒绝学习其背后的数学第一原理，那么我很容易找到。 我相信从事图形工作几年的人很快就会明白这一点。 当要求它编写修复程序时，它提出了一个有效的教科书解决方案，但效率比我从中获得灵感的项目要低得多，尽管克劳德已经在其上下文中解析了源代码。

第二个是 PBR 照明问题，建议我们重写整个照明、移动主光位置并添加环境照明，所有这些都在几个小时后得出结论，其中一项资产的金属/粗糙度纹理有缺陷，并且无论如何更改照明代码都无法正确修复它。 同样，当你自己不是该主题的专家时，你很容易被一个听起来很自信的法学硕士带入徒劳的追逐。

可持续发展

人工智能公司都在亏损。 当然，他们都承诺最终会盈利并获得疯狂的投资回报，但到目前为止他们还没有。 您获得的代币正在赚取边际利润7，但总体而言它们处于亏损状态。 鉴于硬件并没有变得更便宜，而且模型仍然需要一直进行训练，目前看来当前的价格并不可持续。

这就是说，有迹象表明法学硕士未来的费用会变得更高，而不是更低。 就像你可以购买或租用来帮助你工作的每一种工具一样，应该牢记成本与收益的计算，到目前为止，除了强制每个人都使用人工智能的公司之外，似乎还没有发生这种情况，几个月后账单到期时就会收到反指令。

在过去的生活中，我每年都必须为每月花费约 20 欧元的分析工具续订许可证而争论。 从那以后我就听说公司的每个人都订阅了 Claude，甚至包括非程序员。 这是令我困惑的决定。 管理层不会相信工程师会把钱花在他们声称需要的工具上，但随后会告诉每个人他们必须使用他们没有要求的闪亮昂贵的玩具。

对于普通程序员来说，LLM 订阅是否比分析器许可证更通用？ 大概。 我发现加快我不熟悉领域的研究很有用。 如果我一直从事同一个项目，我会每天使用它吗？ 可能不会。 它从根本上改变了我的编码方式吗？ 并不真地。 它会取代程序员吗？ 我认为它不存在，而且在这一点上我严重怀疑它是否会存在。

如果您发现自己经常使用它来编写您并不真正关心的样板代码，那么也许您需要投资更好的 API。
